correctness.rationale: For a fixed support T of twos, precisely the vertices outside T with one neighbor in T are eligible zeros; choosing their labels independently gives z^(14+|T|-|U|)(1+z)^|U|, with a unique lightest labeling. On the Fano bipartition the counts of uniquely incident vertices on the two sides add, followed by subtraction of selected vertices that already have one selected neighbor. All 12 small-support maxima and attaining counts in the frozen table were independently reproduced. Supports of size >=6 weigh at least 12; the table for smaller supports gives minimum 10 only at (1,1),(1,2),(2,1),(2,2). At those sizes equality requires no selected vertex of induced degree one. A nonempty incidence graph on at most two selected points and two selected lines has a degree-one vertex because a four-cycle would give two lines through the same pair of points. Thus equality requires no incidences. There are four lines not incident with a fixed point (and dually), and two distinct lines omit exactly two points, giving 28,42,42,21 labeled supports. Independent exact enumeration by both the 16384 defender subsets and the original adjacency rule on all 4782969 ternary labelings gives all 19 stated nonzero coefficients, total 249827, and checks the full minimum classification and 133 optima, including absence of selected incidences.
residual_risks: Only the fixed labeled Heawood graph, all PRDFs with no extra constraints at positive labels; enumeration is not a statement for other incidence graphs.

value.rationale: The Heawood graph is a canonical cubic incidence graph and the exact weight polynomial is a natural, reproducible benchmark for algorithms counting perfect Roman functions. Its geometric classification gives a reason for equality in the integer cubic upper bound, and identifies all optimal supports with explicit Fano nonincidence types, beyond a single computed number.
residual_risks: The result is specific to Heawood; it is neither a general cubic extremal classification nor a formula for all projective-plane incidence graphs.
